Case study · House of Mews Rescue

Giving a cat rescue complete control over its website

Role
UX/UI Designer & Developer
Client
House of Mews Rescue (nonprofit)
Tools
Figma, WordPress, Elementor Pro
Timeline
4 weeks, Spring 2026

The problem

Adoptable pets came in through a third-party embed, but the rest of the site was static and outdated, so events, “Happy Tails” success stories, and everything else could only be changed by editing code.

What I did

I wireframed a new structure with dedicated, easily scannable layouts for pets, events, and Happy Tails stories, then built it as a dynamically managed site the staff can update themselves.

Context

House of Mews Rescue is a Northeast Ohio nonprofit providing fostering, adoption, and long-term medical care for stray cats and kittens.

This was a full website redesign, moving the rescue from a mostly static, outdated site to a modern, dynamically managed one. Adoptable pet listings already updated automatically through a third-party embed; the redesign gave staff that same independence for events, Happy Tails success stories, and the rest of the site, without touching code.

Constraints

No budget. As a small rescue, House of Mews puts every dollar toward the cats. The new site had to cost less to run than the old one, not just less to build. I donated my time, so the build was free, but ongoing hosting and tools had to fit a nonprofit’s budget.

Non-technical maintainers. The site is maintained by the rescue’s owners, volunteers in their 55+ age range who are comfortable with email and Facebook but not code. Apart from a third-party embed for adoptable cats, every update to the old HTML/CSS site needed a developer. The new one had to let them update adoptable cats, events, and announcements on their own.

Constantly changing content. Adoptable cats come and go weekly. If updates depended on me, the listings would go stale, and stale listings cost adoptions.

Finite volunteer support. I wasn’t on retainer, so the site had to keep working without me. My role after launch needed to be “call if something breaks,” not routine maintenance.
